overview.text: Melanin is a pigment made by melanocytes, specialized pigment-producing cells. It contributes color to skin, hair, and eyes, and is also present in the retina, where it has a role in normal vision. Human melanocytes make two forms, eumelanin and pheomelanin; their relative amounts help shape skin and hair color, with eumelanin associated with brown or black hair and darker skin, and pheomelanin with red or blond hair, freckles, and lighter skin. Eumelanin helps protect skin from ultraviolet damage, while melanin absorbs some harmful rays. Sunlight can stimulate extra melanin production and darken skin, but this protection is incomplete.

key_facts.text: Melanocytes are specialized cells that produce melanin.
Eumelanin and pheomelanin are two forms of melanin; their relative amounts help determine skin and hair color.
Melanin contributes to skin, hair, and eye color; it is also found in the retina, where it plays a role in normal vision.
Eumelanin helps protect skin from UV damage, but melanin does not provide complete protection from the sun.
Sunlight can cause skin to produce more melanin, making it darker; the resulting tan fades as skin cells are replaced.
